items.title: Manny Albam interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998
items.q: except Bill Holman who unfortunately was in Europe at the time.

ctx.x: My name is Monk Rowe. We are filming for the Hamilton College Jazz Archive in Tarrytown, New York, and I’m very pleased to have composer and arranger Manny Albam with me today. I’m going to pick up a thought you just had before the cameras were rolling, and that is retirement has been a busier time than ever for you.

Yeah, it has. I guess I’m more available in a sense. I’m at home more so the phone can ring a little bit more. And for some reason or other I’m getting hot again. I don’t know why. It’s been fun. I’ve been over to Europe many times, I send music over there and I do not have to bring it sometimes but I love to bring it with me. I just came back from L.A. We were in that four-day arranger’s whatever they want to call it — every arranger in the world was out there except Bill Holman who unfortunately was in Europe…

When you say it seems like you’re hot again, do you think your style of writing has changed significantly in the last few years to make you hot again, or is it something that they’re just rediscovering?

items.title: Bill Holman interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, February 13, 1999
items.q: When he was writing for Barnet in 1949 I heard them down in Balboa and they played that, what do you call it, “Swell and Super” a thing, a take off on “Keen and Peachy” that Shorty had done for Woody. And I went home and tried to write a chart something like that.

ctx.x: I think so. So the days of stealing something from Manny Albam or something like that—

Odd you should mention that, because I did that exact thing. When he was writing for Barnet in 1949 I heard them down in Balboa and they played that, what do you call it, “Swell and Super” a thing, a take off on “Keen and Peachy” that Shorty had done for Woody. And I went home and tried to write a chart something like that. But yeah, that’s what you do when you’re young. You try this and you hear something you like and you say I want to try that. And then it just kind of gets absorbed into the whole conception…

items.title: Holman Bill — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I wrote a bunch of charts, and Brookmeyer, and Manny Albam, Marty Paich.

ctx.x: We talked about an early recording with him, but let‟s talk about that tenure with him.

In ‟59 he was working at a club called the Seville down on Santa Monica Boulevard with his quartet. He said – he asked the leader one night. He said, “How would you like a big band to come in here and work all week long for the same money you‟re giving me?” The owner said sure. So Terry, the ultimate businessman, he put all these things together. He had a contract with Mercury to make a big band album. So he said, “We‟ll do the album, use the charts to play on the gig – on our in-person gig.” So we did that. I…

come up with the funniest tunes. One of them was – I think on the first album – was Tico Tico. I think of a lady organ player on The Hit Parade that used to play that, and they‟d always shoot her feet on the pedals. But a jazz chart on Tico Tico? Uh-uh. But I did it, and it came off okay. I wrote some of my best things for that band, I think, in strictly a jazz band vein. Terry – again, the businessman – he wanted a big chord on the end of every chart, whether it called for it or not, regardless of what the song…
